newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish 1997 inflation seen on target despite flood.
newsitem.headline: Polish 1997 inflation seen on target despite flood.

text.p: Poland is likely to meet its ambitious inflation targets this year despite problems created by July's catastrophic floods in the south of the country, the head of the government's centre for strategic studies said.

Zbigniew Kuzmiuk told a news conference on Wednesday that year-on-year inflation in December was likely to ease to 13 percent from 18.5 percent in 1996 and average annual inflation would fall to 15 percent from 19.9 percent in 1996.
In June year-on-year inflation rose to 15.3 percent from 14.6 percent in May, which Kuzmiuk said was a result of a jump in food prices.
"We estimate that year year-on-year inflation in 1997 will be 13 percent and average annual inflation would fall to 15 percent as planned in this year's budget law," he said.
He said the average monthly price growth was likely to slow down to one percent a month in the second half of the year from an average of 1.3 percent in the first half.

Kuzmiuk said inflation would stay under control because overall food prices this year would probably grow more slowly at 10 percent against the planned 12 percent and because of the fast growing imports.
He also noted that the government planned only small official price rises in the second half of the year.

But he said there were also inflationary factors such as the fast growth of wages in the enterprise sector and fast credit growth additionally boosted by flood relief spending, notably by the government loan from the central bank.
He also said the zloty's recent weakening against western currencies and an increase in mandatory social security premiums provided further inflationary impulses.

In June the average wage in the enterprise sector was 27.1 pecent higher than in June 1996 and 6.6 percent higher than in May. Kuzmiuk said the real gross wage rose in the first six months by 5.1 percent while according to the budget law it should have grown only 2.5 percent.

"We expect wage growth in the coming months will stay high, although slightly slower than in the first half," he said, adding the CSS expected the average wage will grow 4.5 percent in real terms in 1997.

Kuzmiuk noted the fast growth of credit for households and companies, which rose 32 percent and 17.2 percent respectively in the seven months ending July 31 and the slowing growth of deposits for households and firms, at 22.4 percent and minus 0.9 percent respectively over the same period.
